paras: The abduction of Walter Saunders was the seizure of a young man from Atchison, Kansas, by a party of men in a Kansas City saloon in March 1882; he was not seen again. His captors accused him of assaulting a thirteen-year-old girl and hurried him toward the Kaw bridge, and it was supposed he had been thrown into the river.

Saunders, called "a popular young citizen of Atchison," had lost his position through drink and gone to Kansas City to clerk in a boot and shoe store. No report gives the race of Saunders or of his captors.

On "last Monday," March 6, Saunders was drinking in a saloon with Edward Toller and others when four men rushed in and dragged him away. The party, grown to twelve, hurried him up a dark alley to a house, where, in the presence of a thirteen-year-old girl named Flanagan, they accused him of assaulting her; he made no reply. He was then hurried toward the Kaw bridge and never heard from again.

According to the Richmond Dispatch, Ellet, "one of two brothers strung up in order to force him to tell what had become of the missing man," said he turned his back when "they made away with him." The report does not say who strung up the brothers.
No report of a body being recovered, of arrests or of an inquest appears in the coverage.

The coverage traces to one Atchison dispatch based on the account of John Kennedy, an eyewitness. The New-York Tribune printed it on March 14 as "Abduction and Probable Murder," and the Richmond Daily Dispatch ran a fuller text on March 15 as "A Young Man Abducted from a Saloon and Not Seen Since." The Democratic Advocate of Westminster, Maryland, condensed it on March 18, placing Saunders in Kansas City, Missouri, and calling his accuser "a young lady." No paper commented or used racial terms.
Where the dispatch gave the drowning as a supposition, the Advocate reported it was "now said" his captors "took him to the river and threw him in."

bases: A group of twelve men seized Saunders, accused him of assaulting a girl and hurried him toward the river, where he was supposed to have been thrown in (A1, A2, A3); his race is not stated, so whether this is anti-Black violence is unknown.

Twelve men seized Saunders without any stated authority after accusing him of assaulting a thirteen-year-old girl (A1, A2), but his death is only supposed from his disappearance near the Kaw bridge and Ellet's statement (A2); no body was reported found.
A1 and A2 print the same Atchison dispatch resting on one eyewitness, John Kennedy, and A3 is a condensed version of the same story rather than an independent report.

accounts.label: Atchison dispatch (John Kennedy, eyewitness)
accounts.gist: Four men, joined by more to twelve, dragged Saunders from a saloon, accused him before a thirteen-year-old girl of assaulting her, and hurried him toward the Kaw bridge; he was supposed thrown into the river.

accounts.label: Ellet's statement
accounts.gist: After being strung up to make him talk, Ellet said he turned his back when 'they made away with' Saunders.

accounts.label: Condensed weekly item
accounts.gist: A young lady charged Saunders with assaulting her, and it was 'now said' his captors took him to the river and threw him in.

framing.detail: The New-York Tribune headed the Chicago-relayed dispatch 'Abduction and Probable Murder.'
The Richmond Dispatch headed it 'A Young Man Abducted from a Saloon and Not Seen Since' and called Saunders 'a popular young citizen of Atchison.'
The Democratic Advocate ran a short unheaded paragraph in 'News of the Week' without comment.

record_check.dossier: Only Walter Saunders; Ellet was one of two brothers strung up by unstated persons to make him tell what became of Saunders, apparently as someone with knowledge of the abduction, and is not reported killed
Not stated in any report; Saunders is called 'a popular young citizen of Atchison' and no racial terms appear
Killing is supposed, not confirmed: he was never heard from and no body was reported found
Seizure and supposed drowning of Saunders; the 'stringing up' was done to the Ellet brothers, not to Saunders, and 'pursuit' was by Saunders's friends following the mob
No county named; A3 places it in Kansas City, Mo.

info: 'Last Monday' in a dispatch dated Monday, March 13, 1882, i.e. Monday, March 6, 1882; A3 says 'a few days since'
